chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from his father, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from al-Minqari, from Hafs ibn Ghiyath, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
'O Hafs! He would forgive seventy sins of the ignorant one before He forgives one sin of the scholar.'

key_terms.الْجَاهِلُ: the ignorant one — one who lacks religious knowledge and acts without awareness
key_terms.الْعَالِمُ: the scholar — one who possesses religious knowledge and is thus held to a higher standard
key_terms.يُغْفَرُ: is forgiven — divine forgiveness, implying this is God's action in the hereafter

ai.seo_question: Why is the sin of a scholar harder to forgive than the sin of an ignorant person?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq addresses Hafs ibn Ghiyath — a distinguished Sunni jurist who narrated from the Imam — with a striking teaching on the elevated moral responsibility of scholars. The hadith conveys that scholarly knowledge, rather than conferring privilege, increases one's accountability before God: seventy sins of an ignorant person may be forgiven before even one sin of a knowledgeable person is forgiven. This reflects the Shia theological principle that knowledge confers hujja (proof/argument), meaning God holds one answerable in proportion to what one knows.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim Bin Hashim, from his father, from Al Qasim Bin Muhammad Bin Al Minqary, from Hafs Bin Giyas, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:
‘O Hafs! He<sup>azwj</sup> would Forgive seventy sins of the ignorant one before He<sup>azwj</sup> Forgives one sin of the scholar’.
en.sarwar: 1. Ali ibn Ibrahim ibn Hashim has narrated from his father from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad from al-Minqari from Hafs ibn Ghiyath from abu ‘Abdallah (a.s.) who has said the following.
“O Hafs, seventy sins of an ignorant person may be forgiven before only one sin of a learned person is forgiven.”
